practiceSet.title: U1.LT4 Practice: Matter, Changes, and Density
practiceSet.description: Practice classifying matter, telling physical from chemical changes, and using density to identify substances.

activity.title: U1.LT4 Relearning: Matter, Changes, and Density
activity.content:
**What you need to be able to do:** I can sort matter into groups (elements, compounds, mixtures), identify physical changes from chemical changes, and use density to figure out what a substance is.

**Everyday analogy:** Think of a school lunch. A single grape is like an **element**: one kind of thing. A peanut butter and jelly sandwich that has been pressed into one new food is like a **compound**: the parts are stuck together and you cannot just pick them apart. A tray with fries, an apple, and milk is a **mixture**: the parts are just sitting together and you can separate them.

**Classifying matter.** **Matter** is anything that has mass and takes up space. All matter is either a **pure substance** or a **mixture**. Pure substances are **elements** (only one type of atom; cannot be broken down by chemical means) or **compounds** (two or more different elements chemically bonded together, like H_{2}O). A mixture is two or more substances physically mixed, not chemically bonded. A **homogeneous** mixture has uniform composition throughout (a **solution**, like salt water). A **heterogeneous** mixture has uneven composition and you can see the parts. A **suspension** has large particles that settle over time and can be filtered out; a **colloid** has medium-sized particles that do not settle.

**Physical vs. chemical change.** A **physical change** does not change what the substance is (melting, cutting, crushing, dissolving). In a **chemical change**, a new substance forms with different properties (burning, rusting, baking). The 5 signs of a chemical change are color change, precipitation, gas production, temperature change, and changes in characteristic properties (odor, light). Add the word **unpredicted** to each sign: mixing paint, shaking a soda, and boiling water show colors, bubbles, or heat, but no new substance forms.

**Density.** Density is the amount of mass per unit of volume: **D = m/v**, in g/mL or g/cm^{3} (1 mL = 1 cm^{3}). Water is 1.00 g/mL; less dense objects float and more dense objects sink. Mass changes with sample size, but density does not, so density can identify a substance. Find volume with **water displacement** (record, drop, record, subtract) or with **L × W × H** for a regular solid.

**Worked example 1:** A metal sample has a mass of 82.8 g. It raises the water in a cylinder from 40.0 mL to 52.0 mL. Volume = 52.0 mL − 40.0 mL = 12.0 mL = 12.0 cm^{3}. D = m/v = 82.8 g ÷ 12.0 cm^{3} = **6.90 g/cm^{3}**. On the table, zinc is 6.90 g/cm^{3}, so the sample is zinc.

**Worked example 2:** A liquid has a density of 1.18 g/mL. What is the mass of 750.0 mL? m = D × v = 1.18 g/mL × 750.0 mL = **885 g**. The mL cancel, leaving grams.

**Worked example 3:** Butter is melted in a pan and then heated until it burns. Melting is a phase change, so the butter is still butter: **physical**. Burning makes black smoke and new substances: **chemical**.

**Watch out for:** flipping the formula to v/m, using the final water level instead of the change, forgetting to subtract the empty cylinder's mass, calling every bubble or color change "chemical," and calling a compound like water a mixture.
prompts: Classify each as an element, compound, homogeneous mixture, or heterogeneous mixture, and explain one: helium, carbon dioxide, sweet tea, vegetable soup.
Hot chocolate powder stirred into hot milk seems to disappear. Is this a physical or chemical change? Use the word "unpredicted" or "new substance" in your answer.
A rock has a mass of 54.0 g and raises the water in a graduated cylinder from 30.0 mL to 50.0 mL. Write the formula, show your setup, and give the density with units.
A block of wood has a density of 0.85 g/cm^{3}. Will it sink or float in water? Explain using numbers.
